• Dietary Modifications (5 marks)
  • • Include naturally gluten-free foods such as fruits, vegetables, legumes, nuts, seeds,
  • meat, poultry, fish, eggs and milk if tolerated.
  • • Replace gluten-containing grains with rice, millet, sorghum, quinoa, buckwheat and
  • amaranth; certified gluten -free oats may be included if uncontaminated and well
  • tolerated.
  • • Limit processed gluten-free foods because they may be high in fat, sugar and salt
  • but low in fibre and essential micronutrients.
  • • Read food labels carefully to identify hidden gluten sources such as wheat star ch
  • and malt, and choose appropriately labelled gluten-free products.
  • • Prevent cross -contamination during storage, preparation and cooking by using
  • separate utensils, cutting boards, toasters and condiment containers when necessary.
  • • Check food preparation pr actices when eating outside the home and ensure

  • dietary intake is inadequate.

questions.question: Describe the procedure for recording and plotting measurements on a WHO Growth Chart.
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the procedure for recording and plotting measurements on a WHO
  • Growth Chart. (1/ (2 mark) for each point)
  • • Select the appropriate WHO growth chart based on the child ’s sex, age, and
  • indicator being assessed, such as weight-for-age or height-for-age.
  • • Accurately measure the child’s weight using a calibrated weighing scale, length for
  • children under 2 years using an infantometer, or height for children aged 2 years
  • and above using a stadiometer.
  • • Plot the measurement by marking the child ’s age on the X -axis and the
  • corresponding anthropometric measurement on the Y-axis.
  • • Record measurements at each follow-up visit, connect consecutive points to form a
  • growth curve, and interpret the pattern using WHO Z -score curves or percentile
  • lines.

questions.question: Describe the different types of dental caries seen in children.
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the different types of dental caries seen in children. (Any 5 points, (1 mark)
  • each)
  • Types of Dental Caries in Children
  • • Early Childhood Caries (ECC): Dental decay in primary teeth, commonly
  • associated with frequent sugar exposure.
  • • Nursing Bottle Caries: Decay caused by prolonged exposure to milk, formula, juice,
  • or other sugary drinks, especially during sleep with a bottle.
  • • Pit and Fissure Caries: Decay in pits and grooves, particula rly on the chewing
  • surfaces of molars.
  • • Smooth Surface Caries: Decay on smooth tooth surfaces due to plaque and
  • prolonged sugar exposure.
  • • Root Caries: Decay affecting exposed tooth -root surfaces; uncommon in young
  • children.
  • • According to stage of development:
  •  Initial/Early Caries: Enamel demineralization appearing as white spots.
  •  Established Caries: Enamel destruction with cavity formation.
  •  Advanced Caries: Decay spreads into dentin and pulp, potentially causing pain and
  • sensitivity.
